LB01.why: Also composes two graph transformations in a stated order, but on a specific quadratic and asks for zeros; here f is unspecified and the asked quantity is the constant gap from swapping a vertical shift and a vertical stretch. Weak match.

LB02.why: Equal outputs at two inputs locate the axis of symmetry of an unknown quadratic; JB16's vertex is a given value, here the vertex lies between table times and needs the leading coefficient from second differences.
Maximum height of a projectile quadratic, but the formula is given there (ACT bank).

LB03.why: Same backward step: a known 2-step growth factor divides out to go back 2 steps (f(x + 2) = 9f(x), f(1) = 6, find f(-1)). Here the 2-year factor must first be found from two values (32,805/40,500), so there is one more step.
Finds a constant percent rate from two values 2 years apart; here the rate is used to work backward instead of being asked.
Runs a known compound rate backward in time; the rate is given there.

LB04.why: Same core computation: a doubling term and a halving term combine by adding or subtracting the exponents t/p. 578 asks when two separate populations become equal (16 = 2^(t/2 + t/6)); here one model multiplies a growth factor by a decay factor and asks the net doubling time. Different asked quantity, so allowed, but do not put both in the same short set.
Variant of the 578 idea (doubles every 2 years, halves every 3 years, ratio 64); same note as for 578.

LB05.why: Inverts an inner linear map to find where a composed function takes a known value (g(x) = f(2x)); here the inner map is 2x - 1 and the answer is a factor. ACT bank, so close only.

LB06.why: Squares a binomial of radicals; 466 is symbolic, here numeric. Different enough.

LB07.why: f(1) = f(9) gives the axis of symmetry of a quadratic; 101 then asks a value at the vertex, here outputs are compared by distance from the axis with a > 0.

LB08.why: Exponential-plus-constant model a·b^x + c fitted from f(0) and f(3), then a value asked (f(2)). 355 gives the base and leaves the constant unknown; here the constant (60) is given and the base is unknown. Same family, different step.
a(0.5)^x + c with the asymptote 6 and intercept 20 given, find f(2); same idea of working with the gap above/below the asymptote, but the base is given there.

LB09.why: Counts intersection points of an absolute-value graph with another graph; there a line with no parameter, here a parabola sharing the vertex, for every a > 0.

LB10.why: Both use the b^x and b^(-x) pair; FB05 uses oddness of 2^x - 2^(-x), here the asked identity is the product. Not a template.

LB11.why: Simplifying a complex fraction built from 1/x terms; different key step (here the sign factor 4 - 2x = -2(x - 2)).

LB12.why: Same function form p(x) = (x - a)(x - b); 153 gives two values and asks a + b, here the vertex is given and ab is asked.
Vertex given, find a combination of coefficients (a + c); different form and asked quantity.

LB13.why: Radical equation with an extraneous root; 145 solves one specific equation, here the root condition is applied across a parameter to count solutions.
Radical equation with a constant, reject the extraneous root; H16 fixes k from a known solution and asks the solution set.

LB14.why: Cubic with unknown coefficients and given zeros; 662 asks the third zero from the constant term, here 0 is the hidden zero and p(-1) is asked.

LB15.why: Rational equation with a parameter where an excluded value (x = 1 there, x = 2 here) changes the solution count; 290 asks for no solution, here exactly one solution arises two ways.
Discriminant = 0 for exactly one real solution; this is only the first of the two cases here.

LB16.why: Area of a triangle whose vertices come from a parabola's intersection points; there the axis intercepts, here the line-parabola intersections plus the origin.
Same intersection of y = x^2 with a line, but asks a distance (ACT bank).

LB17.why: Same sum-of-distances function |x - a| + |x - b|; 204 asks its minimum, here the value is above the minimum and the sum of the two solutions is asked.
Sum of all solutions to an absolute-value equation; single absolute value there.

LB18.why: Set a parabola equal to a line to find where a projectile meets something; there over time with a drone, here in space with a sloped lawn.

LD01.why: Same mechanism: an angle bisector plus a line parallel to a side creates two equal angles (alternate interior / corresponding), forcing an isosceles triangle. JD04 uses an interior bisector and asks a length; here an exterior bisector and an angle is asked.
Same given (angle A = 50 degrees) with bisectors in triangle ABC; interior bisectors of B and C there.

LD02.why: Inscribed angle equals half its intercepted arc; one-step there, here equal chords give equal arcs and the leftover arc is used.

LD03.why: Parallelogram with sides and a 60 degree angle; area there (ACT bank), longer diagonal here.

LD04.why: Triangle areas between parallel lines via shared heights; here P is unknown and the two heights sum to the side length. Weak match.

LD05.why: Circle fixed by tangency to a horizontal line plus points on it; 673 asks the radius, here two parallel tangents give the radius and the asked quantity is the constant c of the expanded equation.
Circle tangent to two lines through a given point, two candidate centers; ACT bank.

LD06.why: Isosceles triangle checked against the triangle inequality; Y05 picks one triangle from two given sides, here all isosceles triangles with perimeter 30 are counted.

LD07.why: Same computation and the same numbers: a length scale factor of 1.5 applied to a measure of 48, so the answer is 48(2.25) = 108, with the identical choice set 72 / 96 / 108 / 162 (the x1.5, x2, x1.5^2 and x1.5^3 traps). Only the wrapper differs (cylinder radius with fixed height vs. photo diagonal). A student who has seen 134 recognizes it immediately.

LD08.why: Shadow similar-triangle problem; point light source there. Different.
Plain sun-shadow proportion (ACT bank); here part of the shadow lies on a wall.

LD09.why: Angular rate of a turning wheel converted to linear speed with a unit change; there via gear teeth and circumference in rpm, here s = r·theta in radians.

LD10.why: Right triangle with tan A = 2 (legs 1 and 2); 480 starts there, here tan A = 2 must be derived from tan A = 4 tan B and the area found from the hypotenuse.
tan A and hypotenuse given, find a leg; one-step version.

LD11.why: Partly filled container whose water region is similar to the full shape (cone at depth 6 of 9); 632 computes the cone volume directly, here the prism means a square law on a ratio.
Water-trough prism capacity; full trough only.

within_list_cues.LB10: Confirmed. A plug-in check eliminates every distractor without the algebra: x = 0 makes f/g = 1, not b^2 (b > 1), which kills C; x = 1 makes f - g = a(b - 1/b) and f + g = a(b + 1/b), both different from 0 and 2a when b > 1, which kills A and B. With any b (say a = 1, b = 2) two numbers settle the item. That is a fair SAT strategy, but for a medium-hard item the key carries no difficulty beyond b^x · b^(-x) = 1. Suggest asking a non-identity quantity (e.g. given f(3)·g(3) or f(k)/g(k), find something), or use distractors that also hold at x = 0 and x = 1.
within_list_cues.LB11: Mild cue: at x = 1 (the only one of 0, 1, 2 in the domain) A, B and D all equal -2, but one more value (x = 3: original -2/3; A -2/3, B -2, C 2/3, D 2/3) separates the key from all three distractors. Two test values are enough. That is normal for an equivalent-expression item; listed for awareness only.
within_list_cues.LB06: Calculator cue: the expression is purely numeric, so evaluating (sqrt 3 + sqrt 12)^2 on the allowed calculator gives 27 directly and no radical simplification is needed. For a medium item that tests radical rules this removes the skill. Consider a symbolic version (e.g. (sqrt(3k) + sqrt(12k))^2 for k > 0, key 27k) or keep it as an easy item.
